name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,127

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Ancient lord administering justice in a family feud

definitions.text: administering justice in a family feud

blocks.note: first meaning: the cast list of Measure for Measure describes this character as 'an ancient lord'

blocks.clueFragment: administering justice in a family feud
blocks.note: second meaning: the Prince of Verona who judges the Montague and Capulet quarrel in Romeo and Juliet

explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare used the name ESCALUS twice: the old lord in Measure for Measure and the Prince of Verona in Romeo and Juliet.
explanation.definitionFit: Both Shakespeare characters carry this name, one an elderly courtier and the other a ruling prince who settles the Verona vendetta.

clue.text: Who the ’eck will Ron Glum marry? An old African?

indicators.note: writing heck with its first letter dropped tells us the reply is spoken in a voice that drops its aitches

blocks.clueFragment: Who the ’eck will Ron Glum marry?
blocks.note: in the radio comedy Take It From Here, Ron Glum's long-suffering fiancée is Eth, so the hopeful reply is 'Eth, I hope' with the h dropped

explanation.surface: An exasperated question about whom a hapless suitor will wed, followed by a puzzled guess about an African.
explanation.walkthrough: The Glums were a 1950s BBC radio sitcom family; Ron was forever engaged to Eth. Say 'Eth, I 'ope' quickly and you get ETHIOPE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethiope is an archaic, chiefly literary term for an Ethiopian or, more loosely, any African person, as in Shakespeare.

clue.text: Here we note general’s position on reserve

blocks.note: general in the sense of shared by all
a position or spot
to reserve a table or seat

explanation.surface: A report on where a general's troops are positioned in the reserve lines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'General' looks like an army officer, but it is an adjective here; the 's is just 'is' joining it on.
explanation.definitionFit: A commonplace book is a personal notebook in which a reader copies out quotations and observations, so it is where we jot things.

clue.text: A learner with a car — a happy man apparently

blocks.note: L is for learner, as on the L-plates of a learner driver
the Austin Allegro was a 1970s British family car

explanation.surface: A learner driver out with a car, looking cheerful about it.
explanation.walkthrough: L'Allegro is Milton's poem paired with Il Penseroso; its title is Italian for 'the cheerful man'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian title literally names a merry or cheerful person, hence 'apparently', since it is really the title of a Milton poem.

clue.text: The Unjust Man or Women in Dawood’s translation

definitions.text: The Unjust Man or Women in Dawood’s translation

blocks.note: surface reading: a choice between a wicked man and some women
setter's reading: these are titles of chapters in N. J. Dawood's English version of the Koran

explanation.surface: Someone weighing up whether a wrongdoer is a man or a group of women, as a translator renders it.
explanation.walkthrough: N. J. Dawood's Penguin Koran gives each chapter an English title; 'Women' is one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A sura is a chapter of the Koran, and each one carries a title such as Women.

clue.text: Child of God’s mostly ill, a week after Christmas

definitions.note: the clue's 's is 'is', joining definition to wordplay

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the final letter of the following word is cut

blocks.note: ill as a noun, meaning damage or hurt
New Year's Day, 1 January, written with the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A believer has been poorly since New Year's Day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A week after Christmas' is a date, 1 Jan, not a span of time.
explanation.definitionFit: Harijan was Gandhi's term for members of the Dalit castes, meaning people of Hari, that is of God.

clue.text: Meet up North, perhaps beside

blocks.note: in Northern English dialect 'happen' means perhaps
upon in the sense of on or by, as a town upon a river

explanation.surface: An invitation to meet somewhere in the North, maybe nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up North, perhaps' is a direction to a dialect: a Yorkshire or Lancashire speaker says 'happen' for perhaps.
explanation.definitionFit: To happen upon someone is to come across or encounter them by chance, which is one sense of meeting.

clue.text: Unusually rare editor – in short, something to do with good books

definitions.text: something to do with good books

indicators.note: unusually suggests the letters are set out in an unusual, non-standard order

blocks.note: taken as written
ED is the short form of editor, as 'in short' says

explanation.surface: A rare editor in brief has a connection with fine literature.
explanation.definitionFit: A favourite book is the kind you return to and go through a second time, so rereading is what you do with one.

clue.text: Curiously half-hearted Jennie’s horseplay seen by one in Hard Times

indicators.note: with half its heart gone, one of the two central matching letters of the name is removed
curiously means in an odd way, telling us the letters are arranged oddly

blocks.note: the name with its possessive s
taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl's rough play, oddly lacking in spirit, is watched by a character from a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Jennie's has a double N at its centre; half-hearted keeps only one N. Horseplay suits her: she rides in Sleary's circus.
explanation.definitionFit: In Dickens's Hard Times, Josephine Sleary is the circus proprietor's daughter and a skilled equestrian performer.

clue.text: Her first words are good sentences, but she suspects they may be ignored

definitions.text: Her first words are good sentences, but she suspects they may be ignored

blocks.clueFragment: Her first words are good sentences
blocks.note: surface reading: a woman who opens with wise remarks

blocks.clueFragment: but she suspects they may be ignored
blocks.note: setter's reading: in The Merchant of Venice Portia's maid opens with advice; Portia calls it 'good sentences', and the maid replies they would be better if well followed

explanation.surface: A sensible woman fears her sound advice will go unheeded.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue paraphrases Act 1 Scene 2 of The Merchant of Venice: 'Good sentences and well pronounced' — 'They would be better if well followed.'
explanation.definitionFit: Nerissa is Portia's waiting-woman in Shakespeare's Merchant of Venice, whose first speech is moralising counsel her mistress praises but doubts she'll follow.

clue.text: Svejk’s introduction to his superiors

blocks.note: surface reading: how a soldier is first presented to his officers
setter's reading: the stock deferential phrase with which Hašek's Good Soldier opens every speech to an officer

explanation.surface: A soldier is presented to his commanding officers.
explanation.walkthrough: Jaroslav Hašek's comic novel The Good Soldier Švejk has its hero begin almost every address to authority with the same servile formula.
explanation.definitionFit: The formula is the English rendering of the Czech military phrase 'poslušně hlásím', which Švejk uses as his opening line to officers.

clue.text: OK about left – a sign of change in Polish letters?

definitions.text: a sign of change in Polish letters

indicators.note: about means around, so the first word wraps round the next

blocks.note: taken as written
left as in departed

explanation.surface: Fine about leaving: is it a signal of change in letters from Poland?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' is capitalised by position: it means from Poland, not shiny. 'Letters' are the alphabet's, not correspondence.
explanation.definitionFit: The ogonek is the little hook beneath a vowel in Polish spelling that marks it as nasal, altering its sound.

clue.text: Oil container held by my Latin or Greek healer and “author”

indicators.note: something held by another is enclosed within it, so one piece sits inside the other

blocks.note: meus is Latin for my
an oil lamp holds oil

explanation.surface: An oil flask kept by a Latin or Greek doctor who also writes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'my Latin' asks for the Latin word for my. Author is in quotes because works on divination were only attributed to him.
explanation.definitionFit: Melampus was the legendary Greek seer and healer, and later treatises on omens circulated under his name.

clue.text: A story-teller from Harris

blocks.note: surface reading: a teller of tales, perhaps a Hebridean one
setter's reading: Harris is not the Scottish island but the American writer Joel Chandler Harris

explanation.surface: A yarn-spinner from the Isle of Harris in the Outer Hebrides.
explanation.walkthrough: Harris looks like the Scottish island famous for tweed; it is the author Joel Chandler Harris.
explanation.definitionFit: Joel Chandler Harris created the elderly narrator who tells the Br'er Rabbit folk tales in his collections.

clue.text: A middle-eastern ambassador sounding pleasant takes in a king and loses nothing

indicators.note: to take something in is to admit it inside, so a letter goes into the word
losing something means it is dropped, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: sweet-sounding
R for rex, Latin for king
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: An envoy from the Middle East with a melodious voice receives a monarch and comes away empty-handed.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes in after EUPH, and the O in the second-last syllable drops out.
explanation.definitionFit: In Antony and Cleopatra, Euphronius is the schoolmaster Antony sends from Egypt as his envoy to Caesar.

clue.text: I’m absorbed by an artist in Italian verse

indicators.note: what is absorbed by something is soaked up inside it

blocks.note: RA, Royal Academician, is a stock abbreviation for an artist
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone engrossed by a painter while reading Italian poetry.
explanation.definitionFit: Rima is Italian for a rhyme or verse, as in terza rima, the interlocking stanza form Dante used.

clue.text: “Barbox Brothers had been some — or irregular branch of the Public Notary and bill-broking tree” (Charles Dickens, Mugby Junction)

definitions.text: “Barbox Brothers had been some — or irregular branch of the Public Notary and bill-broking tree” (Charles Dickens, Mugby Junction)

blocks.clueFragment: Barbox Brothers had been some — or irregular branch
blocks.note: surface reading: a quotation with a word missing, alongside 'irregular branch'

blocks.clueFragment: of the Public Notary and bill-broking tree
blocks.note: setter's reading: the gap needs a word for a side growth of a family tree, the firm being a minor spin-off of a larger business

explanation.walkthrough: The missing word is from the opening of Dickens's Mugby Junction, describing the firm the hero inherits; the tree imagery makes it a side-branch.
explanation.definitionFit: A sideways shoot from a main stem, figuratively a subsidiary body that has grown out of a larger organisation.

clue.text: A poet said to be dull

indicators.note: said means spoken out loud, so we want a word that sounds like the next one

blocks.note: dull as in drab and colourless

explanation.surface: A poet reputed to be boring.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Gray wrote the Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Gray was an eighteenth-century English poet, best known for his Elegy.

clue.text: One of HG Wells’s aliens apparently, one in charge during devastating war

definitions.text: One of HG Wells’s aliens apparently
one in charge during devastating war

blocks.clueFragment: One of HG Wells’s aliens apparently
blocks.note: first meaning: Wells attacked 'an alien and uninspiring court', and the King retorted he might be uninspiring but was damned if he was an alien

blocks.clueFragment: one in charge during devastating war
blocks.note: second meaning: the British monarch throughout the First World War

explanation.surface: A Martian from The War of the Worlds commanding a destructive war.
explanation.walkthrough: HG Wells's aliens suggest The War of the Worlds, but the reference is to Wells's 1917 jibe at the royal family's German origins.
explanation.definitionFit: George V reigned from 1910 to 1936, so was king throughout 1914–18, and changed the dynasty's name to Windsor partly after Wells's taunt.

clue.text: A poet, working in Leopold’s province

blocks.note: Leopold Bloom is the hero of Joyce's Ulysses
province in the sense of area of activity or expertise

explanation.surface: A poet employed in some part of the realm ruled by a king called Leopold.
explanation.walkthrough: Leopold suggests a Belgian king and province a region, but this Leopold is Joyce's, and his province is his field.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Bloomfield was an English rural poet of the Romantic period, author of The Farmer's Boy.

clue.text: The top toy in Jewish culture?

definitions.text: The top toy in Jewish culture?

blocks.note: surface reading: the most popular plaything
setter's reading: top is the kind of toy, a spinning one, played with at Hanukkah

explanation.surface: A question about which plaything is most popular among Jewish children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like 'best', but it names the toy itself: a spinning top.
explanation.definitionFit: A dreidel is a four-sided spinning top marked with Hebrew letters, used in a traditional Hanukkah game.

clue.text: I’m identified by a mole before a murder victim is discovered

definitions.text: I’m identified by a mole before a murder victim is discovered

blocks.note: surface reading: a spy unmasking someone, as in a thriller

blocks.clueFragment: before a murder victim is discovered
blocks.note: setter's reading: in Cymbeline Iachimo describes the heroine's mole on her breast, and later she wakes beside the headless corpse of Cloten

explanation.surface: A spy-thriller narrator is unmasked by an informer just before a body turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mole' looks like a spy, but it is a birthmark: the cinque-spotted mole on her breast that Iachimo reports.
explanation.definitionFit: Imogen is the heroine of Shakespeare's Cymbeline, identified by her birthmark and later finding Cloten's beheaded body.

clue.text: A statement about the gospels that one can make

blocks.note: first meaning: a remark that of the four gospels, one is the one by Mark
second meaning: the idiom 'make ...', to become notable

explanation.walkthrough: Read the first part as 'one is Mark': one of the gospels is Mark's. The second half completes the idiom 'make one's mark'.
explanation.definitionFit: To make an impression or achieve distinction is the familiar idiom, and the same words also observe one of the evangelists is Mark.

clue.text: Confession of a drug dealer: I wanted to poison my lover

definitions.text: I wanted to poison my lover

blocks.note: the admission 'I sold'
E is ecstasy, the drug being traded

explanation.surface: A drug dealer owns up to trying to poison a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: The confession is 'I sold E'. In Wagner's opera she orders a death potion for Tristan, but her maid swaps it for a love potion.
explanation.definitionFit: In Tristan und Isolde she plans to poison Tristan, the man she loves, before the potion is switched.

clue.text: Small vehicle which a rogue apparently made himself in Coriolanus

definitions.text: which a rogue apparently made himself in Coriolanus

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a cab is a taxi

explanation.surface: A little car, which some rascal built for himself in a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: Coriolanus berates the plebeians: 'you dissentious rogues, That, rubbing the poor itch of your opinion, Make yourselves scabs?'
explanation.definitionFit: Coriolanus accuses the rogues of scratching until they turn themselves into scabs, a contemptuous term for low, worthless people.

clue.text: A teller of fantastic stories, Gogol made dancer giddy

indicators.note: giddy means dizzy and whirling, so the letters spin into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The Russian writer Gogol sent a dancer into a spin.
explanation.walkthrough: Gogol himself wrote fantastic stories, which makes him look like the definition; he is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: George MacDonald was a Victorian Scottish author of fantasy novels such as Phantastes and The Princess and the Goblin.

clue.text: Marauding invaders – ones following those like 16?

blocks.note: the number six comes after five, and the answer to 16 ends with a Roman V
16 down is a British monarch

explanation.surface: Raiders, followed by others of the same sort.
explanation.walkthrough: Kings numbered V are followed by those numbered VI, such as George VI after George V.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norse seafaring raiders who plundered the coasts of Britain and Europe from the eighth century.

clue.text: Have a dip? Yes, a long way down in sea water

blocks.note: to bathe or have a bath
an informal way of saying yes
L is the abbreviation for long

explanation.surface: Fancy a swim? Sure, it's deep out in the ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: Oceanographers use bathyal for the deep-sea zone on the continental slope, roughly 200 to 4,000 metres down.
